answer_text:
We want

\[
P=\sum_{n=3}^{42}\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}.
\]

First simplify the summand. Since

\[
\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}2,
\]

we have

\[
\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}
=
\binom{\frac{n(n-1)}2}{2}
=
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{n(n-1)}2\right)\left(\frac{n(n-1)}2-1\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}
=
\frac{n(n-1)\bigl(n(n-1)-2\bigr)}{8}.
\]

Since

\[
n(n-1)-2=n^2-n-2=(n-2)(n+1),
\]

this becomes

\[
\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}
=
\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n+1)}{8}.
\]

But

\[
3\binom{n+1}{4}
=
3\cdot \frac{(n+1)n(n-1)(n-2)}{24}
=
\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n+1)}{8}.
\]

So

\[
\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}=3\binom{n+1}{4}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
P=3\sum_{n=3}^{42}\binom{n+1}{4}.
\]

Let \(k=n+1\). Then as \(n\) runs from \(3\) to \(42\), \(k\) runs from \(4\) to \(43\), so

\[
P=3\sum_{k=4}^{43}\binom{k}{4}.
\]

Using the hockey-stick identity,

\[
\sum_{k=4}^{43}\binom{k}{4}=\binom{44}{5}.
\]

Hence

\[
P=3\binom{44}{5}.
\]

Now compute modulo \(10\):

\[
\binom{44}{5}
=
\frac{44\cdot43\cdot42\cdot41\cdot40}{120}.
\]

Canceling,

\[
\binom{44}{5}
=
44\cdot43\cdot14\cdot41.
\]

Modulo \(10\),

\[
44\cdot43\cdot14\cdot41
\equiv
4\cdot3\cdot4\cdot1
=
48
\equiv
8 \pmod{10}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
P=3\binom{44}{5}\equiv 3\cdot 8=24\equiv 4 \pmod{10}.
\]

\[
\boxed{4}
\]
